a: A siege has been set against us
p: English 5:1 is Hebrew 4:14; English 5:2-15 is Hebrew 5:1-14. The siege is 701 BC or 586 BC.
b: Numbering. The Hebrew Bible ends its chapter 4 with this verse (4:14), so English 5:1 is Hebrew 4:14 and English 5:2-15 is Hebrew 5:1-14. The Greek follows the English numbering. Every reference on this site uses the English numbers. Which siege? Most readers who accept the verse as Micah's own place it in 701 BC, when Sennacherib shut Hezekiah up in Jerusalem (2 Kings 18:13-19:36); the 'judge' is then Hezekiah or his officials. Critical commentators who date chapters 4-5 later point to Babylon's siege (2 Kings 25:1-7), where the king was blinded and led away, and Micah 4:10 names Babylon. The verse itself names neither enemy.

a: Now you will cut yourself
t: Cut yourself, or gather your troops?
p: The Hebrew can mean 'gash yourself in grief' or 'gather in bands'. The 'Daughter of Troops' is probably Jerusalem.
b: The verb titgodedi comes from gadad. In other places the same root means to gash oneself in mourning (Deuteronomy 14:1; Jeremiah 16:6; Jeremiah 41:5), and that is the Plain's reading. But the noun gedud means a raiding band or troop, and the verb can be taken from it: 'gather your troops, city of troops'. The pun (troops, cut) may be on purpose. The 'Daughter' is the city seen as a young woman, as in 'Daughter Zion' (4:8); here most take her to be Jerusalem. The Greek reads quite differently ('the daughter will be walled in with a wall').
orig: תִּתְגֹּדְדִי (titgodedi), 'you will cut yourself' or 'you will gather in troops'

a: the cheek of Israel's judge
t: A struck ruler, and the ruler who comes next
p: To strike a ruler on the cheek is to shame him. The next verse sets a different ruler against him.
b: A blow to the cheek is a public insult (1 Kings 22:24; Job 16:10; Lamentations 3:30). The 'judge' (shofet) is a ruler: the word can name a king or governor (Amos 2:3; Hosea 7:7; 2 Kings 15:5 for Jotham as regent). The Greek reads 'they strike the gates of Israel on the cheek', which suggests the translator read a different word (see the variant). Verses 1 and 2 are a pair: a shamed ruler in a besieged city, and then a ruler who will come from a village. Claude's observation: see the note on 5:2 about why Micah names Bethlehem and not Jerusalem.

a: Bethlehem Ephrathah
p: A small town about six miles south of Jerusalem, David's home. 'Ephrathah' is its older clan name.
b: Bethlehem ('house of bread') lies in the hills of Judah, about six miles (ten kilometers) south of Jerusalem. 'Ephrathah' is the clan or district it belonged to. Rachel was buried 'on the way to Ephrath, which is Bethlehem' (Genesis 35:19). David was 'the son of that Ephrathite from Bethlehem in Judah' (1 Samuel 17:12), and Ruth ends with a blessing on Boaz in 'Ephrathah' and 'Bethlehem' (Ruth 4:11). The town was not among Judah's great cities. By naming it, the prophet points past Jerusalem to David's own beginnings, a king who started as a shepherd boy (2 Samuel 7:8).

a: too small to count among the clans of Judah
p: The Hebrew 'alpe can mean clans or thousands. Matthew's 'leaders' reads the same letters another way.
b: Elep means 'a thousand', and also a clan or military unit of a thousand (Judges 6:15; 1 Samuel 10:19). The Plain translates it 'clans'. If a waw is added, the same letters read alluf, 'chief' (as in Genesis 36:15 for the chiefs of Edom). Matthew's Greek ('leaders', hegemosin) fits the 'chief' reading or a free paraphrase. The Qumran scroll 4Q81 is printed in the transcription with the consonants without the waw, as the Masoretic Text has them; the Murabba'at scroll is damaged at this word. Matthew also turns 'too small' into 'in no way the least', which reverses the sense. See the note on 'From you', and the variant.

a: From you one will come out
t: Matthew 2:5-6 quotes this verse, with changes
p: Matthew's quotation is shorter and reworded. It also adds a line from 2 Samuel 5:2.
b: Matthew's Plain: "And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah, / are in no way the least among the leaders of Judah. / For a leader will come out of you, / one who will shepherd my people Israel." (Matthew 2:6). Differences from the Hebrew: (1) 'land of Judah' for 'Ephrathah'; (2) 'in no way the least' for 'too small'; (3) 'leaders' for 'clans'; (4) Matthew adds 'for' (gar), so that the line gives the reason for the one before; (5) 'a leader' for 'ruler', and the phrase 'to be ruler over Israel' is gone from the line; (6) 'for me' is dropped; (7) 'who will shepherd my people Israel' is not in Micah but in the LORD's word to David, 2 Samuel 5:2, which also supplies the 'ruler over Israel' that Matthew has removed from Micah's line; (8) 'from ancient times' is left out. Matthew's Greek also differs from the Septuagint of Micah. Early Christian readers noticed such differences, and a common answer was that the evangelist gives the sense of the prophet and not his exact words. Most critical readers call it free quotation shaped by Matthew's purpose; a few argue that he knew a different textual or targumic form.

a: to be ruler in Israel
p: A coming king of David's line: a king of Micah's day, a later Davidide, or the Messiah. All readers agree it is a king.
b: Historical. A new David, from David's own town, who will do what the besieged king of verse 1 could not. Commentators of every kind agree it points to a Davidic king; they differ on when he is expected: Hezekiah or a successor, or an unnamed king still to come. Jewish. The Targum Jonathan is reported to render the verse 'from you the Messiah will come out before me' and 'his name was spoken from of old', and Rashi is reported to read the ruler as the Messiah. Neither text was re-read page by page for this note. Ibn Ezra and Kimhi, named in this book's brief, were not checked here, so nothing is claimed about them, about any Jewish reading of a historical king, or about a Jewish reply to Matthew's use of the verse. Christian. Matthew 2:4-6 asks 'where will the Messiah be born?' and answers with this verse; John 7:42 shows that people in Jesus' day expected the Messiah from Bethlehem. Justin Martyr, Origen and Jerome read it of Jesus' birth. Some Christian readers hold a double reference: a king of Micah's own time first, Christ as the full reach of the promise. See the card on this chapter.

a: His origins reach back to the distant past
t: Origins from long ago, or from eternity?
p: The Hebrew says his 'goings out' are from the far past. It does not say he is eternal, but it can be read that way.
b: Motsa'ot means 'goings out', 'origins' or 'comings forth'. Qedem ('the distant past') and 'olam ('long ago, or forever') are both words for distant time; the same words are used of the 'days of old' in 7:14 and 7:20. Readings: (1) David's ancient family line; (2) the ancient divine promise to David (2 Samuel 7); (3) the Messiah's name or plan existing before the world: the Talmud lists 'the name of the Messiah' among seven things made before creation (Pesachim 54a); (4) the eternal Son: many church fathers, including Jerome and Cyril of Alexandria, heard Christ's eternal generation in these words. The Plain keeps the plain-time sense and leaves the larger sense open.
orig: מוֹצָאֹתָיו מִקֶּדֶם מִימֵי עוֹלָם (motsa'otav miqqedem mimei 'olam)

a: From you one will come out
t: Claude's theory: a ruler who does not come from the city
p: Micah names a village, not Jerusalem. That choice matches his attack on Zion's rulers in chapter 3.
b: This is Claude's theory, resting on 3:9-12 and 5:1-2. Micah has said Jerusalem's leaders build Zion with blood (3:10) and that Zion will be plowed (3:12). Verse 1 shows the city's judge struck. Verse 2 then does not hope for a better king from the palace. It looks for a king from the village where David was a shepherd. The point may be that the cure for the rulers is a return to David's beginnings, not a reform of Jerusalem's court. This overlaps with Mays and with Wolff, who both stress the contrast between the royal city and Bethlehem; it is not a new observation, and a reader who takes the passage as Hezekiah-era or exilic can use it equally well.

a: So he will hand them over
p: The verse does not say who hands whom over. The usual reading: the LORD gives Israel up until the birth.
b: Lakhen yitten-em is 'therefore he will give them (up)'. No subject or object is named. (1) The usual reading: the LORD gives his people up to their enemies, the siege of verse 1, for a time, until the 'birth' ends it. (2) A few take the ruler of verse 2 as the subject. The Septuagint has 'he will give them', also without a name. Dispensational readers build on this clause (see the card), taking the 'giving up' as the whole span between Christ's first coming and Israel's regathering. The Plain keeps the pronouns unnamed.

a: a woman in labor gives birth
t: Who is the woman in labor?
p: Some read Zion in labor (Micah 4:9-10), some the ruler's mother; Christians often link Isaiah 7:14 and Mary.
b: 'She who is in labor' is unnamed. (1) Zion or Israel in the pains of exile and return: chapter 4 has already used birth pangs for Zion (4:9-10), and the 'birth' is the end of the exile. (2) The mother of the coming ruler, as in Isaiah 7:14, where a young woman is pregnant and will name a son Immanuel; some commentators link the two verses as two signs for one royal house. (3) Matthew quotes Isaiah 7:14 (Matthew 1:23) and Micah 5:2 (Matthew 2:6) but does not quote 5:3; later Christian readers, for example Jerome, connect the woman of 5:3 with Mary. The Plain has 'a woman in labor' for a Hebrew participle plus perfect; the Hebrew does not say 'virgin'. Whether Micah knew Isaiah's oracle is not provable; they were contemporaries (Micah 1:1; Isaiah 1:1).

a: the rest of his brothers will come back
p: The 'brothers' are most likely the ruler's fellow Israelites who return from exile.
b: The Hebrew has 'the rest of his brothers will return to (or with) the Israelites'. The 'rest' (yeter) of the ruler's brothers are those still left, the remnant of 4:7 and 5:7-8. The idea of a king whose 'brothers' are his people is Deuteronomy's ideal (Deuteronomy 17:15, 20). 'Return' (shuv) is the book's word for coming back from exile, and the preposition can mean 'to join' or 'to'. The Septuagint says 'will turn to the sons of Israel', which can hint at repentance.
orig: וְיֶתֶר אֶחָיו יְשֻׁבוּן עַל־בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל (veyeter echav yeshuvun 'al-bene Yisra'el)

a: shepherd them
p: Shepherd is the Bible's picture of a ruler who feeds, guards and leads. The Hebrew gives no object here.
b: In the ancient Near East kings were called shepherds. The LORD tells David, "You are the one who will shepherd my people Israel" (2 Samuel 5:2). Ezekiel 34 blames Israel's shepherds for feeding themselves and promises one shepherd, 'my servant David' (Ezekiel 34:23). Micah has used the picture before (2:12) and will use it again (5:5; 7:14). The Hebrew verb stands alone, 'he will stand and shepherd'; the Greek adds 'his flock', and Matthew 2:6 adds 'my people Israel' from 2 Samuel 5:2. The ruler shepherds 'in the strength of the LORD', so the rule is borrowed, not his own.
r: 2 Samuel 5:2; 2 Samuel 7:7; Ezekiel 34:23; Psalm 80:1; Micah 2:12; Micah 7:14

a: This one will be peace
p: 'Peace' (shalom) is not only calm: it is wholeness and safety. The ruler himself is called by it.
b: The Hebrew is short: vehayah zeh shalom, 'and this one will be peace'. English versions divide it differently: some close verse 4 with it, some begin verse 5 with it, and the Vulgate reads 'he will be peace'. The word shalom covers safety, wholeness and well-being. The ruler 'is' peace, as Isaiah 9:6 calls the coming son the 'Prince of Peace' and Zechariah 9:10 promises a king who speaks peace to the nations. The next words show that this peace is not the end of conflict at once: Assyria is still coming. The letter to the Ephesians (2:14) says Jesus 'is our peace', and the Christian reading hears Micah's line fulfilled in him.
orig: וְהָיָה זֶה שָׁלוֹם (vehayah zeh shalom), 'and this one will be peace'

a: If Assyria enters our land
t: Assyria in Micah's lifetime, and after
p: Assyria threatened Judah from 734 BC. It reached Jerusalem's gate in 701. Some readers take 'Assyria' as a name for any later empire.
b: Judah became Assyria's vassal under Ahaz (2 Kings 16:7-10). Hezekiah's rebellion brought Sennacherib's army in 701 BC, which took the walled towns of Judah (2 Kings 18:13) and shut up Jerusalem; the angel of the LORD struck the Assyrian camp (2 Kings 19:35). That is the natural setting for 5:5-6 if Micah wrote it. A second view: after Assyria fell (612 BC) 'Assyria' became a code for the enemy empire of any age (compare Ezra 6:22, where the Persian king is called 'king of Assyria'). Verse 6 gives 'Nimrod's land', which can also stand for Babylon (Genesis 10:10).

a: seven shepherds
p: 'Seven and eight' is a poet's way of saying 'a full number and more'. Later Jews gave the numbers names.
b: Counting 'seven, even eight' is a Hebrew way to say 'enough and more than enough', as in Amos 1:3 'for three rebellions, and for four' and Proverbs 6:16 and Job 5:19 (see the topic Numerical Sayings). Micah does not give names. The Talmud (Sukkah 52b) does: seven shepherds, who are Adam, Seth, Methuselah, Abraham, Jacob and Moses, with David in the middle; and eight princes, listed as Jesse, Saul, Samuel, Amos, Zephaniah, Hezekiah, Elijah and the Messiah. Some editions read Zedekiah in the place of Hezekiah. That list is a rabbinic reading, not what Micah says. Modern commentators take the numbers as a figure of speech for a large number of capable leaders.

a: shepherd the land of Assyria
p: The verb 'shepherd' (ra'ah) can also be read 'rule harshly' or 'crush'. The Plain keeps 'shepherd'.
b: The same Hebrew letters can be read as 'shepherd' (ra'ah) or as 'shatter, ruin' (ra'a'); Psalm 2:9 has the same ambiguity ('break them with an iron rod' in the Hebrew, 'shepherd them with an iron rod' in the Greek). Here the Greek translates 'shepherd'; the Vulgate reads 'shepherd' too; many modern translations and commentators choose 'rule' or 'devastate' because of 'with the sword'. A shepherd with a sword is not strange: David the shepherd killed lions and a giant. The Plain keeps the book's own picture (5:4; 7:14).
orig: וְרָעוּ (vera'u), 'they will shepherd' or 'they will shatter'

a: the land of Nimrod
p: 'Nimrod' is the hunter-king of Genesis 10, linked with Babylon and Assyria's cities. Micah uses it as another name for Assyria.
b: Genesis 10:8-12 says Nimrod was 'a mighty hunter', that his kingdom began in Babel (Babylon), Erech and Akkad in Shinar, and that 'from that land' he or Asshur went out to build Nineveh, Calah and other cities (the Hebrew allows either 'he went out to Assyria' or 'Asshur went out'). Micah's 'land of Nimrod' is parallel to 'the land of Assyria', so it names the same land from its legendary founder. Nothing outside the Bible names a king Nimrod of Assyria; scholars have compared him with the Assyrian king Tukulti-Ninurta I, with Sargon of Akkad and with the god Ninurta, and none is proven.

a: like dew from the LORD
t: The remnant as dew, and as a lion
p: Dew and showers give life to a field; the lion tears. The two pictures of the remnant are placed side by side.
b: The remnant of Jacob (5:7-8) is given two pictures. Dew is a gift from the LORD that waters the grass without human help (Hosea 14:5; Deuteronomy 32:2). Then comes the lion, which tramples and tears. Readings: (1) a blessing to the nations and a danger to those who resist, each in turn; (2) two sides of one reality, with the remnant a source of life to those who accept it and a threat to those who do not (compare Genesis 12:3); (3) the dew is the exiles' hope and the lion their victory over oppressors. 'Remnant' is a key word in Micah (2:12; 4:7; 7:18); see the topic on the remnant. Paul draws on Isaiah's remnant in Romans 9:27 and 11:5.

a: which put no hope in anyone
p: Dew and rain do not wait for human permission. The sentence says the remnant's life comes from God, not from human help.
b: The relative clause 'which does not hope for (qavah) anyone or wait for (yachal) human beings' is about the dew and showers, which come when the LORD sends them. Applied to the remnant, it means their rescue does not depend on human powers, which fits 5:10-11 where the LORD removes their horses and fortresses. Some read it otherwise: the remnant will not need the nations' approval, or the nations will not be able to hold the remnant back. 'Hope' and 'wait' are the book's own verbs for trust in the LORD (7:7, yachal), so the human-help reading is the likeliest.

a: a young lion
t: The lion: Judah, Balaam and Micah's own oracle
p: The lion picture of Israel is old: Jacob blesses Judah as a lion, and Balaam calls Israel a lion.
b: Jacob's blessing calls Judah 'a lion's cub' (Genesis 49:9). Balaam, the same Balaam who is named in 6:5, sees Israel as a lion that does not lie down until it has eaten its prey (Numbers 23:24; compare Numbers 24:9). Micah does not quote Balaam, but putting 5:8 and 6:5 in one chapter invites the link: the pagan seer who was hired to curse ended by blessing. The picture is hard: the lion tramples and tears, and no one can rescue the prey. Readers who take 5:7-8 as promise accept that; some commentators hear a threat to the nations that mistreated Israel.

a: I will cut off your horses from your midst
t: Horses and chariots: the cleansing of trust in weapons
p: The LORD removes what Judah trusted for safety: horses, chariots, fortresses, magic and idols.
b: From here the 'you' is Judah itself, not the nations. The verb 'cut off' (karat) is repeated five times (verses 10-14) and the Plain keeps it every time. Horses and chariots were a king's modern army; Deuteronomy 17:16 forbade a king to multiply horses, and Isaiah 31:1 condemns those who rely on Egypt's horses. Psalm 20:7 says 'some trust in chariots'. So the 'day' removes military trust (verses 10-11), then religious trust in magic and images (verses 12-14). Zechariah 9:10 has the same promise for the coming king: 'I will cut off the chariot from Ephraim'. A day of the LORD that purifies his own people is the book's third kind of day.

a: sorceries
p: The two words are named in Deuteronomy 18:10 among the practices Israel must not copy from the nations.
b: Keshafim is 'sorceries' and me'onenim is people who read signs (Deuteronomy 18:10, 14). The Plain of Deuteronomy has 'works sorcery' (18:10) and 'read signs' (18:10, 14); Micah's Plain uses the matching nouns 'sorceries' and 'sign-readers', so the link is visible. Isaiah 2:6 says Judah is 'full of' practices from the east and of soothsayers like the Philistines. King Manasseh later practiced all of this (2 Kings 21:6), which is one reason scholars who date Micah 5:10-15 late see it as a response to his reign. The prophets never treat magic as a harmless folk custom: it is a different source of power and information from the LORD.

a: standing stones
p: Standing stones marked Canaanite shrines. The law forbade them; Hezekiah smashed them.
b: A standing stone (matsevah) was an upright stone set up at a shrine. The law told Israel to shatter the Canaanites' stones (Deuteronomy 12:3) and not to set up one of their own (Deuteronomy 16:22). Hosea 3:4 and 10:1-2 list them among the northern kingdom's practices. Hezekiah, in Micah's own time, 'smashed the standing stones' (2 Kings 18:4). At Arad and Beer-sheba, excavators found a shrine and an altar that had been taken apart, buried or reused in later walls. Some link this with Hezekiah's reform and others with Josiah's; the dating is disputed. 'Carved images' are the idols the stones stood beside.

a: Asherah poles
p: An Asherah pole was a wooden post or tree at a shrine. Why 'cities' stands beside it is unclear.
b: Asherim are the poles or trees linked with the goddess Asherah (Deuteronomy 16:21; 2 Kings 18:4; 1 Kings 16:33 for Ahab's). Hezekiah cut one down (2 Kings 18:4). The last half of the verse, 'and demolish your cities', sits oddly beside poles. Some scholars suspect a different word; the Masoretic Text, the Septuagint and the Murabba'at scroll (which preserves the letters for 'your cities' here) all read 'cities', so no witness supports a change, and the Plain keeps 'cities'. Possibly the cities are the local shrine towns where such objects stood.

a: I will carry out vengeance
t: Vengeance on the nations that did not listen
p: 'Vengeance' (naqam) is God setting right a wrong. Its target is the nations that refused to listen, not Israel.
b: The Hebrew naqam is not private revenge. It is a ruler's act of justice, putting right what was wrongly done (Deuteronomy 32:35, 41, 43). The Plain keeps 'vengeance' for it. Here the object is 'the nations that have not listened', a verb (shama') that means both 'hear' and 'obey', and the one the book began with ('Hear, all you peoples', 1:2). Nahum 1:2 uses the same word for the LORD against Nineveh, and Nahum is the next book of the Twelve. The cleansing in verses 10-14 is of Israel; here the same God addresses the nations.

a: Listen, please, to what the LORD is saying
p: Chapter 6 opens a third speech with 'Hear'. It is a courtroom scene: the LORD sues his own people.
b: Micah has three speeches that begin with a call to hear (1:2; 3:1; 6:1), and each turns from judgment toward hope. This one is cast as a lawsuit (Hebrew riv): a plaintiff, a defendant, witnesses and a charge. Other prophets use the same pattern: Isaiah 1:2-20 (heaven and earth as witnesses), Hosea 4:1, Jeremiah 2:4-13, and the long poem of Deuteronomy 32, which also opens by calling heaven and earth. The speaker in 6:1-2 is the prophet: he is told to 'argue your case' and then announces 'the LORD has a case against his people' (6:2, the LORD in the third person). The LORD himself speaks in the first person from 6:3. Whether this is a fixed legal form is debated (de Roche questions it); see the note on 6:2.
r: Micah 1:2; Micah 3:1; Isaiah 1:2; Hosea 4:1; Jeremiah 2:4; Deuteronomy 32:1

a: with the mountains
p: In ancient treaties, mountains and rivers were called as witnesses. Here the hills hear Israel's case.
b: Near Eastern treaties between kings call the gods, and also mountains, rivers, springs and the great sea, as witnesses; the Hittite treaties are the best known. Israel's covenant texts keep the pattern but replace the many gods with heaven and earth (Deuteronomy 4:26; 30:19; 31:28; 32:1). Micah picks mountains and hills: they were there when Israel entered the land and they will outlast the court (6:2). Their silence is part of the charge. Psalm 50:4 and Isaiah 1:2 use heaven and earth as the court. The Hebrew has 'et before 'the mountains', which usually means 'with'; so 'argue your case with the mountains' is literal, and 'before the mountains' (the usual English) is a decision that the mountains are the audience. Either way the mountains hear.

a: has a case against his people
p: Scholars call this pattern the 'covenant lawsuit'. Some now doubt it was a fixed form.
b: The key word is riv ('case, quarrel, dispute'), the term the Plain renders 'case' and 'bring a case' (Hosea 2:2; 4:1; 12:2). In 1959 Herbert Huffmon proposed that the prophets copied a legal form in which the LORD, as the offended king, accuses his vassal Israel. G. Ernest Wright applied it to Deuteronomy 32. Others, such as Michael de Roche (1983), argue that riv is a wider word for any dispute and that no single formal genre is shown. Even those who doubt the form agree that Micah 6:1-8 reads like a courtroom dialogue.

a: Testify against me
t: Answer me, or testify against me?
p: The Hebrew verb can mean 'answer' or 'testify against'. The Greek and Vulgate read 'answer me'.
b: "Ane bi can mean 'answer me" (the Septuagint and the Vulgate) or 'testify against me' (the verb 'anah followed by be is a witness's phrase, as in Deuteronomy 19:16 for a false witness and Numbers 35:30 for a witness). In a courtroom, the LORD invites any charge: 'What did I do to wear you out?' The question shows the LORD has acted, not abused. The next two verses answer it with the Exodus and Balaam, which are the best 'testimony' for the defense.
orig: עֲנֵה בִי (aneh vi), 'answer me' or 'testify against me'

a: Moses, Aaron and Miriam
t: Miriam named with Moses and Aaron
p: This is the only place in the prophets where Miriam is named as a leader sent by the LORD.
b: The Exodus is the LORD's first evidence (Exodus 20:2): 'I brought you up from the land of Egypt', words also in Amos 2:10 and Hosea 12:13. Micah adds three leaders: Moses, Aaron and Miriam. She is the prophet who led the women in the song at the sea (Exodus 15:20), and her name appears with theirs in a sense of shared leadership; in Numbers 12 she and Aaron challenge Moses and she is struck with skin disease, and in Numbers 20:1 her death is recorded. Micah 6:4 is the only time a prophet names her. The Septuagint keeps her. Jewish tradition (Bavli Taanit 9a) remembers the well that followed Israel for Miriam's merit; that is a later teaching.

a: the plan of Balak king of Moab
p: Balak hired Balaam to curse Israel. Balaam blessed them instead, then led them into sin at Peor.
b: The story is in Numbers 22-24. Balak king of Moab sent for Balaam son of Beor, a seer from the River, to curse Israel (Numbers 22:5-6). Balaam's oracles blessed Israel instead, as Balak complained: 'you have blessed them and blessed them again, these three times!' (Numbers 24:10). The 'answer' Balaam gave is those blessings. But the Bible has a darker memory: Israel's seduction by Moabite women at Shittim (Numbers 25:1), and Moses' charge that it was 'on Balaam's advice' (Numbers 31:16); Revelation 2:14 calls it the teaching of Balaam. Micah's list is short; he chooses the part of the story in which God turned a curse to blessing. The topic on Balaam gives the later readings.
r: Numbers 22:5; Numbers 24:10; Numbers 25:1; Numbers 31:16; Deuteronomy 23:4; Joshua 24:9

a: from Shittim to Gilgal
p: The Hebrew has no verb here. Shittim is the last camp east of the Jordan, Gilgal the first camp west of it.
b: The phrase stands without a verb, so it may name a topic ('and what happened from Shittim to Gilgal') or the rest of the 'answer' to Balaam. Shittim (Abel-shittim) is where Israel camped before crossing the Jordan and where Balaam's plan led to sin (Numbers 25:1; 33:49; Joshua 3:1). Gilgal is where Israel camped just after the crossing and where the LORD rolled away the disgrace of Egypt (Joshua 4:19; 5:9). So the list takes the people from the last stop before the land to the first inside it, the miracle of the Jordan between. Some see the list as a short creed of what the LORD did for Israel.

a: the right things the LORD has done
p: 'Tsidqot' is a plural. It names acts by which the LORD put things right for his people.
b: Tsidqot YHWH are 'the righteous acts of the LORD': the times he did what was right by his people and for them (Judges 5:11, 'the righteous acts of the LORD', the victories of the song of Deborah; 1 Samuel 12:7; Psalm 103:6). The Septuagint has a single 'righteousness'. Elsewhere this site renders tsedaqah 'righteousness' and 'what is right'; here the plural is spelled out as 'right things', so the English hears them as deeds, not as a quality. The point of the history lesson is that Israel's own account of its past is a list of what the LORD did right.

a: Should I meet him with burnt offerings
t: The worshipper's questions, and the prophets on sacrifice
p: The questions escalate: calves, then thousands of rams, then a child. The answer in verse 8 is not 'no sacrifice'.
b: Verses 6-7 are the worshipper's reply: how far must I go to please God? The offerings grow: year-old calves (the usual burnt offering, Leviticus 9:3), then thousands of rams and rivers of oil, then a firstborn child. The answer, 6:8, sets 'justice, loyal love and humility' against this. Other prophets speak the same way: Isaiah 1:11-17; Amos 5:21-24; Hosea 6:6; and so do psalms (Psalm 40:6; Psalm 50:8-15; Psalm 51:16-17) and 1 Samuel 15:22. Readings: (1) the prophets reject sacrifice without justice, not sacrifice itself; (2) they reject the system (Wellhausen's older view); (3) 'not this but that' as a Hebrew way to say 'this more than that'.
r: Leviticus 9:3; Isaiah 1:11; Amos 5:21; Hosea 6:6; Psalm 40:6; Psalm 51:16; 1 Samuel 15:22

a: Shall I give my firstborn for my rebellion
t: The firstborn, and child sacrifice in Judah
p: The speaker offers his own child. Child sacrifice happened in Judah in Micah's own day, under Ahaz.
b: Ahaz, in Micah's lifetime, 'made his son pass through the fire' (2 Kings 16:3); Manasseh did so later (2 Kings 21:6) and Josiah ended it at Topheth (2 Kings 23:10). The LORD says of it, "I never commanded it" (Jeremiah 7:31), and the law forbids it (Leviticus 18:21; 20:2; Deuteronomy 18:10). A king of Moab in a tight spot offered his firstborn on a wall (2 Kings 3:27). The law also says every firstborn belongs to the LORD and must be bought back, not given (Exodus 13:2, 13). The verse may be rhetoric, the last step of an argument by exaggeration, or it may name a practice the hearers knew. The binding of Isaac (Genesis 22) is the other biblical story of a father and a child; it ends with the child spared.
r: 2 Kings 3:27; 2 Kings 16:3; 2 Kings 21:6; Jeremiah 7:31; Leviticus 18:21; Exodus 13:13; Genesis 22:12

a: to do justice, to love loyal love
p: Mishpat is acting rightly in the community; hesed is loyal, faithful love shown in deeds. Both are things you do.
b: Mishpat ('justice') is the right ordering of life together, above all in courts and for the weak. Hesed is the faithful love that keeps a promise; this site renders it 'loyal love'. 'To love hesed' is unusual: Hosea 6:6 and 12:6 pair the same two ideas, and Zechariah 7:9 puts justice, hesed and compassion together. Many English Bibles say 'love mercy' (the Septuagint has eleos, 'mercy'), which is close but loses the idea of loyalty. Compare the Exodus-creed that ends the book (7:18-20): the LORD delights in hesed (7:18), and here he asks his people to love it too.
orig: עֲשׂוֹת מִשְׁפָּט וְאַהֲבַת חֶסֶד (asot mishpat ve'ahavat hesed)

a: to walk with your God in humility
p: The Hebrew word for 'humility' is very rare. 'Humbly', 'modestly' and 'with care' are all defended.
b: Hatsne'a lekhet is an infinitive absolute of tsana', a verb that appears only here in the Bible. Its adjective tsanua' names 'the modest' in Proverbs 11:2 ('wisdom stays with the modest'). Rabbinic Hebrew uses tsni'ut for modesty and privacy. So the Plain says 'in humility'. A few scholars take the root as 'carefully, attentively' (the Greek has hetoimon einai, 'be ready to walk with'). The Talmud (Sukkah 49b) reads it as doing quiet acts: burying the dead and escorting a bride, matters done discreetly. All readings fit a life lived beside God and not for show. See the variant.

a: he has told you what is good
t: The Talmud: 613 commandments reduced to three
p: In the Talmud, Rabbi Simlai says Micah reduced the 613 commandments to three.
b: Bavli Makkot 23b-24a says the Torah has 613 commandments. David reduced them to eleven (Psalm 15), Isaiah to six (Isaiah 33:15-16), Micah to three (this verse), Isaiah again to two (Isaiah 56:1), and Amos and Habakkuk to one each ('Seek me and live', Amos 5:4; 'the righteous will live by his faith', Habakkuk 2:4). The passage is a homily on how the commandments can be summed up; it does not say the others are optional. Sukkah 49b explains the three: justice, acts of loving-kindness, and walking modestly. Compare the way Jesus names 'the heavier things in the law: justice, mercy and faithfulness' (Matthew 23:23).

a: What is the LORD asking from you?
p: Jesus' charge about the 'heavier things in the law' repeats Micah's three. Luke names justice and the love of God.
b: In Matthew 23:23 Jesus says the scribes and Pharisees 'pay a tithe on mint and dill and cumin, but you have let go of the heavier things in the law: justice, mercy and faithfulness'. The three nouns match Micah's three in sense: justice, mercy (the Greek eleos is the Septuagint word for hesed here), and faithfulness. Luke 11:42 has 'justice and the love of God'. Matthew 9:13 and 12:7 quote Hosea 6:6 in the same spirit. The New Testament does not say Micah is the source; the connection is one of theme. Deuteronomy 10:12-13 asks for more than three things, so Micah's 'only' is a summary of the covenant's heart.

a: sound wisdom
t: A hard verse: 'sound wisdom sees your name'
p: Verse 9 is one of the hardest in the book. The Hebrew has a rare word, 'tushiyyah', and an odd verb.
b: Tushiyyah is a rare word in Job, Proverbs and Isaiah, meaning something like 'sound wisdom' or 'success'. The sentence 'sound wisdom sees your name' could mean 'wisdom is to see (fear) your name', as the Greek has 'he will save those who fear his name'. Another view moves one letter to read 'it is wisdom to fear your name' (the Vulgate has 'salvation will be for those who fear your name'). The Plain keeps the Masoretic text and says the line is difficult. Most commentators think the verse begins the new section and that 'the voice of the LORD' calls the whole city to pay attention.

a: Listen, tribe, and whoever appointed it
t: Tribe or rod? Who appointed it?
p: 'Mateh' means both 'tribe' and 'rod'. 'Who appointed it?' is also hard.
b: Mateh is a word for 'rod, staff' and also 'tribe' (the one who holds a staff). Three readings: (1) 'tribe' (the Plain: Judah or the city is addressed); (2) 'rod': listen to the punishment and the one who has appointed it (most modern versions, with a small change in the vowels); (3) 'the rod' of Assyria, which Isaiah calls the rod of the LORD's anger (Isaiah 10:5). "Whoever appointed it" (u-mi yi'ad-ah) can mean 'who has set it' (the rod, the punishment) or 'who has set the appointed time'. The Greek has 'who will adorn the city?', a different division of the letters.
orig: שִׁמְעוּ מַטֶּה וּמִי יְעָדָהּ (shim'u matteh u-mi yi'adah)

a: a skimpy ephah
p: An ephah is a dry measure of about 22 liters. A skimpy one is a cheat. The law forbade it.
b: An ephah was a standard dry measure of about 22 liters (around two-thirds of a bushel). A seller who used a smaller ephah to measure grain for the buyer, or a heavier weight to weigh silver, cheated. The law says "Have scales that are right, weights that are right, an ephah that is right" (Leviticus 19:36), and calls cheating with two sets 'abhorrent to the LORD' (Deuteronomy 25:13-16). Amos 8:5 speaks of those who 'make the ephah small and the shekel large'; Proverbs 11:1 and 20:10 say the LORD hates dishonest weights. Stone weights marked with their values have been found in Judean sites from Micah's time. For Micah, this is a charge of fraud against the poor, like 2:1-2.
r: Leviticus 19:35; Deuteronomy 25:13; Amos 8:5; Proverbs 11:1; Proverbs 20:10; Micah 2:2

a: a bag of false weights
p: Merchants carried their weights, stone discs, in a pouch. A buyer could not see which stone was used.
b: Weights were stones carried in a bag: the LORD 'made every stone in the bag of weights' (Proverbs 16:11), and the law says not to keep two kinds of weights 'in your bag' (Deuteronomy 25:13). A merchant could keep one stone for buying and a lighter one for selling. The prophets put this crime beside violence: 6:12 says the same city's rich people are 'full of violence'. The LORD's question in 6:11 is whether he, the judge, could count this as clean. The Plain has 'Can I be clean with wicked scales'; the Greek and Vulgate turn it into a question about acquitting the cheat (see the variant).

a: I in turn will make you sick
t: 'I too will make you sick' or 'I have begun to strike'
p: The Hebrew verb can come from 'be sick' or 'begin'. The Greek reads 'begin'.
b: Hecheleti is read as a form of chalah ('be sick', hiphil 'make sick'; compare Isaiah 53:10). The Greek has 'I will begin to strike you', which suggests the root chalal ('begin'), and the Vulgate reads 'I have begun to strike you'. The difference is a vowel. Either way the LORD answers the city's wrongs with sickness and ruin. The Plain's 'in turn' renders gam ani, 'I also': the city struck others, and now it is struck.
orig: הֶחֱלֵיתִי (hecheleti), 'I will make sick'; or הַחִלֹּתִי (hachilloti), 'I have begun'

a: You will sow, yet reap nothing
p: The punishment list matches the curses of Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28: work done, fruit taken.
b: The pairs in 6:14-15 (eat but not be full, sow but not reap, tread olives but not be anointed with oil, make wine but not drink it) are the covenant curses: Deuteronomy 28:30-40 says you will plant a vineyard and not enjoy it, you will tread olives but not anoint yourself, and Leviticus 26:26 says you will eat and not be satisfied. Amos 5:11 and Zephaniah 1:13 use the same lines; Haggai 1:6 uses them of the people who neglect the Temple. The same words that were promised as a blessing (Leviticus 26:3-5) are reversed. The LORD brings what the covenant said he would.

a: all the works of the house of Ahab
t: Omri and Ahab: why these two
p: Omri founded Samaria's dynasty; his son Ahab was the king of Baal worship and Naboth's murder.
b: Omri (about 885-874 BC) built Samaria and made the northern kingdom a power; he 'did worse than all who were before him' (1 Kings 16:25). The Mesha stele (Moab) names 'Omri king of Israel', and Assyrian records call the northern kingdom 'the house of Omri', so his name was known across the region. His son Ahab married Jezebel, 'took up the service of Baal' (1 Kings 16:31) and, with Jezebel, took Naboth's vineyard by a false trial (1 Kings 21), the kind of land-grab Micah attacks in 2:1-2. Judah's own kings had a house of Ahab connection through Athaliah (2 Kings 8:18, 26). The verse says Judah is keeping their rules. The Hebrew verb is rare and may be a passive (see the variant).

a: a thing to hiss at
p: 'Horror' and 'hissing' are fixed words for a ruined place that makes onlookers gasp.
b: Shammah ('horror, desolation') and sheriqah ('hissing, whistling') are a pair for a place so ruined that passers-by whistle in shock, a stock phrase in Jeremiah (Jeremiah 19:8; 25:9, 18) and in Chronicles (2 Chronicles 29:8). The Plain uses the same two English words each time. 'You will bear the disgrace of my people' reverses their expected honor as the LORD's people. The Greek has 'peoples' (see the variant).

a: Woe to me!
p: The speaker is the prophet, the city, or the community. The cry 'alelay' is a different word from 'hoy'.
b: 'Alelay li is a rare cry of grief (Job 10:15 has it). It is not hoy ('Woe to...'), the prophet's word of warning (2:1; compare Isaiah 5:8). Readings: (1) Micah himself, a lone honest man (7:2, 7); (2) Zion personified (the 'enemy' of 7:8 and 7:10 speaks to her); (3) the righteous remnant of Judah. The speaker will shift: lament (7:1-6), trust (7:7), confession (7:8-9), promise (7:11-13), prayer (7:14), reply (7:15) and praise (7:18-20). Hermann Gunkel (1924) read the end of the book as a kind of liturgy with several voices.

a: the gathering of summer fruit
p: Gleaning is picking up what the harvesters missed. Micah finds no grapes and no fig left.
b: In the harvest the owner left what he missed for the poor (Leviticus 19:9-10; Deuteronomy 24:21). The speaker is the gleaner who comes late and finds nothing: not even one cluster or one early fig (Hosea 9:10 uses early figs for a nation's first good fruit). The image is of a land in which not a single loyal person is left for him to find (7:2). Jeremiah searched Jerusalem for one person (Jeremiah 5:1) and Elijah thought he was alone (1 Kings 19:10, 14). The reader who knew the book's first chapters would remember that the people had taken the poor's fields (2:2).

a: The loyal have vanished from the land
p: 'Chasid' is a person who lives by hesed, loyal love. Psalm 12:1 opens with the same complaint.
b: The chasid is the loyal person, the one who keeps hesed to God and to neighbors. Psalm 12:1 says the same thing: 'the loyal one has come to an end'. The complaint is that the community has no one left who could do what 6:8 asks. 'Upright' (yashar) is the second word, and then the whole land becomes a hunting ground: they 'lie in wait for blood' and hunt a brother with a net. Compare 3:1-3, where the rulers 'eat my people's flesh'.

a: the judge wants a bribe
p: A corrupt court was the main way the poor lost their land. The prophet has already named the judges.
b: The Hebrew has the official 'asking' (for a payment), the judge '(asking) for the bribe' (shillum, 'a payment, a gift in return'), and the great man 'speaking the craving of his own self'. The law forbade bribes because they 'blind the eyes of the wise' (Exodus 23:8; Deuteronomy 16:19). Micah 3:11 had already said 'her leaders judge for a bribe'. The last phrase, 'they braid it together' (ya'abotuha), uses the image of twisting strands into one rope: official, judge and rich man work as one plait. See the variant for the Greek's different text.
orig: הַשָּׂר שֹׁאֵל וְהַשֹּׁפֵט בַּשִּׁלּוּם (hasar sho'el vehashofet bashillum)

a: The day your watchmen spoke of
p: Watchmen warn of coming danger. In the prophets the word often means the prophets themselves.
b: Ezekiel is told "I have set you as a watchman for the house of Israel" (Ezekiel 3:17; 33:2-7), and Jeremiah 6:17 says 'I set watchmen over you'. Habakkuk takes his stand on the watchtower (Habakkuk 2:1). So 'the day of your watchmen' is the day the prophets announced, the day of the LORD's visit (pequddah, 'punishment, visitation'). Isaiah 56:10 is the complaint that some watchmen are blind. Micah says the announced day has now come, and 'confusion' (mevukhah, panic) will start. This recalls the false prophets of 3:5-7, who said 'peace' and now have nothing to say. The Greek at the end of 7:3 and the start of 7:4 reads differently, with a first-person line, 'I will take away their good things'; see the variant at 7:3.

a: Do not believe a neighbor
p: Even home is not safe: not a neighbor, a friend or a wife. Jeremiah 9:4-5 speaks the same way.
b: Jeremiah 9:4 says, 'Everyone must guard against his neighbor.' Psalm 41:9 speaks of a close friend who betrays. The Hebrew 'close friend' (alluf) is a word for a trusted companion (Psalm 55:13). The final warning is the sharpest: be careful what you say even to 'her who lies in your bosom', the wife. This is the opposite of the covenant community, in which a man could trust his neighbor (Leviticus 19:17-18). The verse prepares for 7:6.

a: The people of a man's own household are his enemies
t: Matthew 10:35-36 and Luke 12:53 take up this verse
p: Jesus says his coming divides households and uses Micah's words. The Mishnah also uses them for the time before the Messiah.
b: In Matthew 10:35-36 Jesus says: "I came to set a man at odds with his father, a daughter with her mother, and a daughter-in-law with her mother-in-law. Those in a man's own house will be his enemies." Matthew's last line is close to the Septuagint of Micah ('a man's enemies' and 'his household') and he adds a verb of his own, 'to set at odds' (literally 'to split'). Luke 12:53 adds father against son and gives each pair both ways round. The Mishnah (Sotah 9:15) quotes Micah 7:6 among the signs of 'the footsteps of the Messiah'. The two uses agree that family division marks the end of an age. In Micah the division is moral breakdown; in Jesus' mouth it is the result of choosing him. See the topic on discipleship.

a: I, though, will keep watch for the LORD
t: The turn from lament to trust
p: The 'I, though' marks a sharp turn. After the verses about broken trust, the speaker trusts God.
b: The pronoun va'ani ('and I', 'but as for me') sets the speaker against the whole society of 7:1-6. 'Keep watch' (tsafah) is the watchman's verb of 7:4, now used for the speaker's own stance: the watchmen of Judah did not warn, but he watches. 'Wait' (yachal) is the book's verb for trust (5:7). 'The God who saves me' is 'elohe yish'i, which sounds like the name Joshua/Jesus (yeshua', 'the LORD saves'); some Christian readers have heard the name of Jesus in such phrases, as Jerome's Vulgate does at Habakkuk 3:18. The Hebrew only says 'God of my salvation'.

a: Enemy of mine
p: The Hebrew 'enemy' is feminine. It is probably a city or nation personified.
b: 'Oyavti is the feminine form, so the enemy is a woman: either a city (as nations are called 'Daughter X') or a nation personified. Candidates are Babylon (4:10), Edom (compare Obadiah, Psalm 137:7), or an unnamed power. In 7:10 she says 'Where is the LORD your God?', the taunt the nations used in exile (Psalm 79:10; Joel 2:17). A reading as Samaria is less likely since Samaria had fallen. The Plain keeps the unnamed 'enemy'; the chapter's picture is of a power that gloats while the speaker sits in the dark.

a: until he takes up my case and does me justice
p: The speaker admits guilt and trusts the same LORD who has a case against Israel (6:2) to defend him against the enemy.
b: Here the lawsuit of chapter 6 is turned around. The LORD who has a case against his people (6:2) will, after the punishment, argue the speaker's case against the enemy: 'until he takes up my case' (yarib ribi). The speaker does not claim to be innocent; he carries the LORD's anger because 'I have sinned'. Compare Psalm 43:1, Jeremiah 50:34 and Lamentations 3:58, where the LORD takes up a cause. "His righteousness" (tsidqato) is the same word as 'the right things' of 6:5: the LORD's own faithful acts of setting things right.

a: Where is he, the LORD your God?
p: 'Where is your God?' is what scorners said to exiles. Psalms 42:3, 79:10 and Joel 2:17 repeat it.
b: The taunt is a way of saying God has failed or is absent. Psalm 42:3, 10 puts it in a worshipper's mouth; Psalm 79:10 and 115:2 ask God to answer it, and in Joel 2:17 the priests pray that the peoples will not be able to say it. Micah says this taunt will be answered when the speaker sees the enemy 'trampled like street mud'.

a: On that day the boundary will lie far away
p: 'Chok' can mean a boundary or a decree. The 'walls' are the fences of a vineyard or sheepfold.
b: Gader (plural gederot) is the stone wall around a vineyard or a sheepfold (Isaiah 5:5; Numbers 32:16), so 'build your walls' fits the shepherd picture of 7:14. Chok is 'boundary' or 'decree'; the Vulgate has 'the law will be far away' and others read 'the decree' (against Zion) is distant. Two readings: (1) the walls are rebuilt after exile and the borders will be pushed far out (the Plain); (2) the boundary or decree that kept Israel small will be removed. Nehemiah's rebuilding of the walls is often linked with the first reading (Nehemiah 2:17). The Greek is quite different (see the variant).

a: Egypt's cities
t: Matsor: Egypt, a fortress or Tyre?
p: The Hebrew 'matsor' can be a poetic name for Egypt, the word for 'fortress', or sound like 'Tyre'.
b: Matsor is a poetic name for Egypt (Isaiah 19:6; 37:25; 2 Kings 19:24), related to Mitsrayim. It is also the ordinary word for 'siege' or 'fortress' (as in 5:1). The Greek reads 'your fortified cities' and 'from Tyre to the river' (Tyre = Tsor), so the Septuagint also loses Egypt. The Plain follows the Masoretic Text: people come from Assyria in the east and Egypt in the south, from Egypt to the River (the Euphrates), from sea to sea and mountain to mountain. This is the picture of Psalm 72:8 and Zechariah 9:10: the borders of David's empire (Genesis 15:18). See the variant.
orig: עָרֵי מָצוֹר (arei matsor), 'cities of Egypt' (or 'fortified cities')

a: the earth will turn into a wasteland
t: 'But the earth' - a break in the promise
p: After a promise of gathering, verse 13 speaks of ruin. It may be about the nations' lands, or Judah's before the gathering.
b: Verse 13 begins 'But', and it is hard to say what it contrasts with. (1) The ruin of the lands of those who resisted, the opposite of the gathering to Zion (7:12). (2) Judah's own land, ruined for its people's deeds (6:13, 16), as the necessary prelude to the day of 7:11. (3) A break between separate pieces, on the view that 7:11-13 and 7:14-20 came from different hands. The Hebrew 'earth/land' (erets) allows both 'earth' and 'land'. The result of deeds ('the fruit of their deeds') matches the Plain of 7:13 and the book's moral theme.

a: Be a shepherd to your people with your rod
t: A prayer for the shepherd's care
p: The speaker asks the LORD to shepherd as the ruler of 5:4 did. The prayer asks for the old days.
b: Here the shepherd is the LORD himself, asked to care for the flock he owns ('your inheritance'). Psalm 28:9 prays 'Shepherd them, and carry them for all time', and the rod and staff of Psalm 23:4 are the shepherd's tools. The 'rod' (shevet) is also the rod of counting (Leviticus 27:32) and of the ruler's scepter (Genesis 49:10). The prayer asks the LORD to be what the human shepherds of Israel were not, the same wish as Ezekiel 34. In 5:4 a human shepherd stands 'in the strength of the LORD'; here the LORD is the shepherd. The Christian reading finds both in Jesus (John 10:11).

a: in the middle of orchards
p: 'Karmel' is both the mountain on the coast and the common word for orchard land.
b: Karmel is the name of Mount Carmel, and also an ordinary word for 'orchard' or 'garden land' (Isaiah 29:17; 32:15; Jeremiah 4:26). The Greek takes it as the mountain ('in the middle of Carmel'). The context decides: the flock lives 'by themselves in a forest, in the middle of orchards', so 'orchards' fits, and then 'Bashan and Gilead', the high pastures east of the Jordan (Numbers 32; Deuteronomy 3:13-17). A flock that lives alone is the picture of Numbers 23:9, 'a people that lives alone', and of Deuteronomy 33:28.

a: I will show them wonders
p: The voice changes to the LORD's. The Hebrew says 'I will show him', meaning Israel as one person.
b: The LORD answers the prayer, speaking in the first person: 'I will show him wonders.' The Plain has 'them', since 'him' is Israel as a single person (the 'you' of the prayer is also singular). 'Wonders' (nifla'ot) is the Exodus word (Exodus 3:20; 34:10; Psalm 78:11-12). The promise is a new Exodus. The Septuagint has 'you will see wonders'. The Murabba'at scroll preserves the Hebrew of 7:15 and agrees with the Masoretic Text.

a: They will lick up dust like a snake
p: To lick dust is to bow before a conqueror. The nations are made low like the serpent of Eden.
b: Psalm 72:9 prays that the king's enemies 'lick the dust' and Isaiah 49:23 says kings will 'lick up the dust of your feet'. The snake was cursed to eat dust (Genesis 3:14). The picture is complete submission. The last lines, 'they will come in dread to the LORD our God, and they will fear you', are either the nations' conversion (compare 4:1-2) or their fear as defeated enemies. The Hebrew does not say which; both readings have defenders.

a: Who is a God like you
t: A pun on the prophet's name
p: 'Micah' (Mikhayahu) means 'Who is like the LORD?'. The book ends by asking that question and answering it.
b: The prophet's name means 'Who is like Yah (the LORD)?'. The book of Micah has the short form Mikhah in 1:1; in Jeremiah 26:18 the Hebrew written text (the ketiv) has the longer Mikhayah (read aloud Mikhah), and a still longer Mikhayahu is the form for other men of the name, as in Judges 17. The question mi-El kamokha (7:18) is the name turned into a question. It echoes the Song of the Sea: "Who is like you among the gods, O LORD?" (Exodus 15:11), and Isaiah 40:25, Psalm 113:5. The Exodus song asks about God's power over Egypt; Micah's asks about his willingness to forgive.

a: who forgives guilt and passes over the rebellion
t: The creed of Exodus 34:6-7 in Micah
p: Micah uses the great creed of Exodus 34 but keeps only the forgiving half.
b: The creed the LORD proclaimed to Moses says he is 'slow to anger, great in loyal love and faithfulness' and is 'forgiving guilt, rebellion and sin' (Exodus 34:6-7). Micah takes up the words 'forgiving guilt' (nose' 'avon), 'rebellion' (pesha'), 'anger' and 'loyal love' (hesed), and ends with hesed and 'faithfulness' (7:20). He leaves out the line 'he will by no means leave guilt unpunished'. Other prophets quote the creed differently. Jonah 4:2 and Joel 2:13 use the gracious half and add 'he changes his mind about the harm', which Micah does not. Nahum 1:3 in this site's Plain reads 'slow to anger, his power is great' (it swaps 'loyal love' for 'power') and adds that he will not leave the guilty unpunished. Micah also takes up the root of 'compassion' (rachem, 7:19), a word of the creed in Exodus 34:6. This is one of the 'creed' texts across the Twelve, which shape each book's last word.
r: Exodus 34:6; Exodus 34:7; Numbers 14:18; Jonah 4:2; Joel 2:13; Nahum 1:3

a: He will not hold on to his anger forever
t: A closing creed for the Twelve, and the Shabbat Shuvah
p: Psalm 103:9 says the same. Jews read these verses on the Sabbath between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur.
b: 'He will not hold on to his anger forever' resembles Psalm 103:9 ('he will not nurse his anger for all time'). The verses 7:18-20 are the haftarah (the reading from the prophets) for the Sabbath between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, called Shabbat Shuvah ('the Sabbath of return', from Hosea 14:2, 'Return, Israel'), in many rites, together with Hosea 14:2-10 (some rites add Joel 2:15-27). For the Christian reading, see the card on 7:19. In the Hebrew order Micah is the sixth of the Twelve, and its closing creed leads on to Nahum, which uses the same words in a harsher sense (Nahum 1:2-3).

a: He will subdue our guilt
p: 'Kavash' means to subdue by force. Guilt is treated like an enemy beaten underfoot.
b: Kavash means to subdue or to bring under one's foot (Genesis 1:28; Joshua 18:1; 2 Samuel 8:11). Guilt ('avon) is pictured as an enemy the LORD overcomes, like the nations in 7:17. Many English Bibles say 'tread underfoot', which fits the second picture of throwing sins into the sea: first the enemy is pinned, then it is thrown into the depths. The Greek has 'he will sink our guilt'. The person changes in the Hebrew from 'he' to 'you' in the same verse (a common shift in prayers), and the Plain keeps that change; in the Greek the sins are the subject of a passive verb, so that shift is in the Hebrew only. The Hebrew also says 'all their sins' after 'our guilt' and 'us'; the Greek and the Latin say 'our'. See the second variant.

a: Into the depths of the sea
t: The sea that drowned Egypt now drowns sins; tashlich
p: The same word for 'depths' is used when Pharaoh's army sinks in Exodus 15. Jews cast crumbs into water at Rosh Hashanah.
b: Metsulot ('depths') is the word in Exodus 15:5, where the Egyptians 'went down to the bottom like a stone'. The sea that took the oppressors now takes Israel's sins. This verse is the source of the custom of tashlich ('you will throw'), observed on the afternoon of the first day of Rosh Hashanah at a body of water, where Jews say Micah 7:18-20 and symbolically cast away sins. The custom is medieval: it is reported in the customs of the Maharil (Rabbi Jacob Moellin; sources differ on his dates) and in the notes of Moses Isserles, and the casting of crumbs belongs to later practice. Its origin is debated. In the Roman lectionary, the Saturday of the second week of Lent reads Micah 7:14-15, 18-20 with Luke 15:1-3, 11-32, the parable of the prodigal son. See the card.

a: faithfulness to Jacob
t: Faithfulness to Jacob, loyal love to Abraham
p: The book ends on the promise to the fathers. 'Faithfulness' and 'loyal love' are the creed's two words.
b: 'Faithfulness' (emet) and 'loyal love' (hesed) are the pair the LORD gave in Exodus 34:6. Jacob and Abraham stand for the whole people and the promises made to them: Abraham's blessing and land (Genesis 12:1-3; 22:16-18) and the promise to Jacob at Bethel (Genesis 28:13-15). Psalm 105:9-10 makes the same link. Zechariah's song in Luke 1:72-73 recalls 'the oath he swore to Abraham our father'. The prophet ends where the book of Genesis started the promises: the future depends on what the LORD swore, not on Israel's record.

a: loyal love to Abraham
t: Claude's theory: the Exodus frames chapters 6-7
p: The Exodus appears at the start of chapter 6, the middle of chapter 7, and the end. It may be the book's closing frame.
b: This is Claude's theory, resting on 6:4, 7:15, 7:19 and 7:20. The Exodus comes up three times in the last two chapters: as the first evidence in the LORD's lawsuit (6:4), as the promise of 'wonders' like the days of the Exodus (7:15), and in the 'depths' where Egypt's army sank (7:19). The closing oath to the fathers (7:20) is what the Exodus itself rested on. The effect would be to answer the lawsuit's accusation with the promise it began from. Scholars have noticed the Exodus echoes in 6:4 and 7:15; I have not seen the whole set claimed as a frame, so treat it as a suggestion.
